121 def alias(selectable, name=None, flat=False):

186 def tablesample(selectable, sampling, name=None, seed=None):

224      REPEATABLE sub-clause is also rendered.

228         sampling, name=name, seed=seed)

571     def correspond_on_equivalents(self, column, equivalents):
572         """Return corresponding_column for the given column, or if None
573         search for a match in the given dictionary.

584     def corresponding_column(self, column, require_embedded=False):
585         """Given a :class:`.ColumnElement`, return the exported
586         :class:`.ColumnElement` object from this :class:`.Selectable`
587         which corresponds to that original
588         :class:`~sqlalchemy.schema.Column` via a common ancestor
589         column.
590 
591         :param column: the target :class:`.ColumnElement` to be matched
592 
593         :param require_embedded: only return corresponding columns for
594          the given :class:`.ColumnElement`, if the given
595          :class:`.ColumnElement` is actually present within a sub-element
596          of this :class:`.FromClause`.  Normally the column will match if
597          it merely shares a common ancestor with one of the exported
598          columns of this :class:`.FromClause`.
599 
600         """
601 
602         def embedded(expanded_proxy_set, target_set):
603             for t in target_set.difference(expanded_proxy_set):
604                 if not set(_expand_cloned([t])
605                            ).intersection(expanded_proxy_set):
606                     return False
607             return True
608 
609         # don't dig around if the column is locally present
610         if self.c.contains_column(column):
611             return column
612         col, intersect = None, None
613         target_set = column.proxy_set
614         cols = self.c._all_columns
615         for c in cols:
616             expanded_proxy_set = set(_expand_cloned(c.proxy_set))
617             i = target_set.intersection(expanded_proxy_set)
618             if i and (not require_embedded
619                       or embedded(expanded_proxy_set, target_set)):
620                 if col is None:
621 
622                     # no corresponding column yet, pick this one.
623 
624                     col, intersect = c, i
625                 elif len(i) > len(intersect):
626 
627                     # 'c' has a larger field of correspondence than
628                     # 'col'. i.e. selectable.c.a1_x->a1.c.x->table.c.x
629                     # matches a1.c.x->table.c.x better than
630                     # selectable.c.x->table.c.x does.
631 
632                     col, intersect = c, i
633                 elif i == intersect:
634 
635                     # they have the same field of correspondence. see
636                     # which proxy_set has fewer columns in it, which
637                     # indicates a closer relationship with the root
638                     # column. Also take into account the "weight"
639                     # attribute which CompoundSelect() uses to give
640                     # higher precedence to columns based on vertical
641                     # position in the compound statement, and discard
642                     # columns that have no reference to the target
643                     # column (also occurs with CompoundSelect)
644 
645                     col_distance = util.reduce(
646                         operator.add,
647                         [sc._annotations.get('weight', 1) for sc in
648                          col.proxy_set if sc.shares_lineage(column)])
649                     c_distance = util.reduce(
650                         operator.add,
651                         [sc._annotations.get('weight', 1) for sc in
652                          c.proxy_set if sc.shares_lineage(column)])
653                     if c_distance < col_distance:
654                         col, intersect = c, i
655         return col
656

724     def _populate_column_collection(self):

732     def _refresh_for_new_column(self, column):
733         """Given a column added to the .c collection of an underlying
734         selectable, produce the local version of that column, assuming this
735         selectable ultimately should proxy this column.
736 
737         this is used to "ping" a derived selectable to add a new column
738         to its .c. collection when a Column has been added to one of the
739         Table objects it ultimtely derives from.
740 
741         If the given selectable hasn't populated its .c. collection yet,
742         it should at least pass on the message to the contained selectables,
743         but it will return None.
744 
745         This method is currently used by Declarative to allow Table
746         columns to be added to a partially constructed inheritance
747         mapping that may have already produced joins.  The method
748         isn't public right now, as the full span of implications
749         and/or caveats aren't yet clear.
750 
751         It's also possible that this functionality could be invoked by
752         default via an event, which would require that
753         selectables maintain a weak referencing collection of all
754         derivations.
755 
756         """
757         if not self._cols_populated:
758             return None
759         elif (column.key in self.columns and
760               self.columns[column.key] is column):
761             return column
762         else:
763             return None

933     @classmethod
934     def _join_condition(cls, a, b, ignore_nonexistent_tables=False,
935                                 a_subset=None,
936                                 consider_as_foreign_keys=None):
937         """create a join condition between two tables or selectables.
938 
939         e.g.::
940 
941             join_condition(tablea, tableb)
942 
943         would produce an expression along the lines of::
944 
945             tablea.c.id==tableb.c.tablea_id
946 
947         The join is determined based on the foreign key relationships
948         between the two selectables.   If there are multiple ways
949         to join, or no way to join, an error is raised.
950 
951         :param ignore_nonexistent_tables:  Deprecated - this
952         flag is no longer used.  Only resolution errors regarding
953         the two given tables are propagated.
954 
955         :param a_subset: An optional expression that is a sub-component
956         of ``a``.  An attempt will be made to join to just this sub-component
957         first before looking at the full ``a`` construct, and if found
958         will be successful even if there are other ways to join to ``a``.
959         This allows the "right side" of a join to be passed thereby
960         providing a "natural join".
961 
962         """
963         constraints = cls._joincond_scan_left_right(
964             a, a_subset, b, consider_as_foreign_keys)
965 
966         if len(constraints) > 1:
967             cls._joincond_trim_constraints(
968                 a, b, constraints, consider_as_foreign_keys)
969 
970         if len(constraints) == 0:
971             if isinstance(b, FromGrouping):
972                 hint = " Perhaps you meant to convert the right side to a "\
973                     "subquery using alias()?"
974             else:
975                 hint = ""
976             raise exc.NoForeignKeysError(
977                 "Can't find any foreign key relationships "
978                 "between '%s' and '%s'.%s" %
979                 (a.description, b.description, hint))
980 
981         crit = [(x == y) for x, y in list(constraints.values())[0]]
982         if len(crit) == 1:
983             return (crit[0])
984         else:
985             return and_(*crit)
986 
987     @classmethod
988     def _joincond_scan_left_right(
989             cls, a, a_subset, b, consider_as_foreign_keys):
990         constraints = collections.defaultdict(list)
991 
992         for left in (a_subset, a):
993             if left is None:
994                 continue
995             for fk in sorted(
996                     b.foreign_keys,
997                     key=lambda fk: fk.parent._creation_order):
998                 if consider_as_foreign_keys is not None and \
999                         fk.parent not in consider_as_foreign_keys:
1000                     continue
1001                 try:
1002                     col = fk.get_referent(left)
1003                 except exc.NoReferenceError as nrte:
1004                     if nrte.table_name == left.name:
1005                         raise
1006                     else:
1007                         continue
1008 
1009                 if col is not None:
1010                     constraints[fk.constraint].append((col, fk.parent))
1011             if left is not b:
1012                 for fk in sorted(
1013                         left.foreign_keys,
1014                         key=lambda fk: fk.parent._creation_order):
1015                     if consider_as_foreign_keys is not None and \
1016                             fk.parent not in consider_as_foreign_keys:
1017                         continue
1018                     try:
1019                         col = fk.get_referent(b)
1020                     except exc.NoReferenceError as nrte:
1021                         if nrte.table_name == b.name:
1022                             raise
1023                         else:
1024                             continue
1025 
1026                     if col is not None:
1027                         constraints[fk.constraint].append((col, fk.parent))
1028             if constraints:
1029                 break
1030         return constraints
1031 
1032     @classmethod
1033     def _joincond_trim_constraints(
1034             cls, a, b, constraints, consider_as_foreign_keys):
1035         # more than one constraint matched.  narrow down the list
1036         # to include just those FKCs that match exactly to
1037         # "consider_as_foreign_keys".
1038         if consider_as_foreign_keys:
1039             for const in list(constraints):
1040                 if set(f.parent for f in const.elements) != set(
1041                         consider_as_foreign_keys):
1042                     del constraints[const]
1043 
1044         # if still multiple constraints, but
1045         # they all refer to the exact same end result, use it.
1046         if len(constraints) > 1:
1047             dedupe = set(tuple(crit) for crit in constraints.values())
1048             if len(dedupe) == 1:
1049                 key = list(constraints)[0]
1050                 constraints = {key: constraints[key]}
1051 
1052         if len(constraints) != 1:
1053             raise exc.AmbiguousForeignKeysError(
1054                 "Can't determine join between '%s' and '%s'; "
1055                 "tables have more than one foreign key "
1056                 "constraint relationship between them. "
1057                 "Please specify the 'onclause' of this "
1058                 "join explicitly." % (a.description, b.description))
1059 
1060     def select(self, whereclause=None, **kwargs):
1061         r"""Create a :class:`.Select` from this :class:`.Join`.
1062 
1063         The equivalent long-hand form, given a :class:`.Join` object
1064         ``j``, is::
1065 
1066             from sqlalchemy import select
1067             j = select([j.left, j.right], **kw).\
1068                         where(whereclause).\
1069                         select_from(j)
1070 
1071         :param whereclause: the WHERE criterion that will be sent to
1072           the :func:`select()` function
1073 
1074         :param \**kwargs: all other kwargs are sent to the
1075           underlying :func:`select()` function.
1076 
1077         """
1078         collist = [self.left, self.right]
1079 
1080         return Select(collist, whereclause, from_obj=[self], **kwargs)

1086     @util.dependencies("sqlalchemy.sql.util")
1087     def alias(self, sqlutil, name=None, flat=False):
1088         r"""return an alias of this :class:`.Join`.
1089 
1090         The default behavior here is to first produce a SELECT
1091         construct from this :class:`.Join`, then to produce an
1092         :class:`.Alias` from that.  So given a join of the form::
1093 
1094             j = table_a.join(table_b, table_a.c.id == table_b.c.a_id)
1095 
1096         The JOIN by itself would look like::
1097 
1098             table_a JOIN table_b ON table_a.id = table_b.a_id
1099 
1100         Whereas the alias of the above, ``j.alias()``, would in a
1101         SELECT context look like::
1102 
1103             (SELECT table_a.id AS table_a_id, table_b.id AS table_b_id,
1104                 table_b.a_id AS table_b_a_id
1105                 FROM table_a
1106                 JOIN table_b ON table_a.id = table_b.a_id) AS anon_1
1107 
1108         The equivalent long-hand form, given a :class:`.Join` object
1109         ``j``, is::
1110 
1111             from sqlalchemy import select, alias
1112             j = alias(
1113                 select([j.left, j.right]).\
1114                     select_from(j).\
1115                     with_labels(True).\
1116                     correlate(False),
1117                 name=name
1118             )
1119 
1120         The selectable produced by :meth:`.Join.alias` features the same
1121         columns as that of the two individual selectables presented under
1122         a single name - the individual columns are "auto-labeled", meaning
1123         the ``.c.`` collection of the resulting :class:`.Alias` represents
1124         the names of the individual columns using a
1125         ``<tablename>_<columname>`` scheme::
1126 
1127             j.c.table_a_id
1128             j.c.table_b_a_id
1129 
1130         :meth:`.Join.alias` also features an alternate
1131         option for aliasing joins which produces no enclosing SELECT and
1132         does not normally apply labels to the column names.  The
1133         ``flat=True`` option will call :meth:`.FromClause.alias`
1134         against the left and right sides individually.
1135         Using this option, no new ``SELECT`` is produced;
1136         we instead, from a construct as below::
1137 
1138             j = table_a.join(table_b, table_a.c.id == table_b.c.a_id)
1139             j = j.alias(flat=True)
1140 
1141         we get a result like this::
1142 
1143             table_a AS table_a_1 JOIN table_b AS table_b_1 ON
1144             table_a_1.id = table_b_1.a_id
1145 
1146         The ``flat=True`` argument is also propagated to the contained
1147         selectables, so that a composite join such as::
1148 
1149             j = table_a.join(
1150                     table_b.join(table_c,
1151                             table_b.c.id == table_c.c.b_id),
1152                     table_b.c.a_id == table_a.c.id
1153                 ).alias(flat=True)
1154 
1155         Will produce an expression like::
1156 
1157             table_a AS table_a_1 JOIN (
1158                     table_b AS table_b_1 JOIN table_c AS table_c_1
1159                     ON table_b_1.id = table_c_1.b_id
1160             ) ON table_a_1.id = table_b_1.a_id
1161 
1162         The standalone :func:`~.expression.alias` function as well as the
1163         base :meth:`.FromClause.alias` method also support the ``flat=True``
1164         argument as a no-op, so that the argument can be passed to the
1165         ``alias()`` method of any selectable.
1166 
1167         .. versionadded:: 0.9.0 Added the ``flat=True`` option to create
1168           "aliases" of joins without enclosing inside of a SELECT
1169           subquery.
1170 
1171         :param name: name given to the alias.
1172 
1173         :param flat: if True, produce an alias of the left and right
1174          sides of this :class:`.Join` and return the join of those
1175          two selectables.   This produces join expression that does not
1176          include an enclosing SELECT.
1177 
1178          .. versionadded:: 0.9.0
1179 
1180         .. seealso::
1181 
1182             :func:`~.expression.alias`
1183 
1184         """
1185         if flat:
1186             assert name is None, "Can't send name argument with flat"
1187             left_a, right_a = self.left.alias(flat=True), \
1188                 self.right.alias(flat=True)
1189             adapter = sqlutil.ClauseAdapter(left_a).\
1190                 chain(sqlutil.ClauseAdapter(right_a))
1191 
1192             return left_a.join(right_a, adapter.traverse(self.onclause),
1193                                isouter=self.isouter, full=self.full)
1194         else:
1195             return self.select(use_labels=True, correlate=False).alias(name)
1196

1443     def cte(self, name=None, recursive=False):
1444         r"""Return a new :class:`.CTE`, or Common Table Expression instance.
1445 
1446         Common table expressions are a SQL standard whereby SELECT
1447         statements can draw upon secondary statements specified along
1448         with the primary statement, using a clause called "WITH".
1449         Special semantics regarding UNION can also be employed to
1450         allow "recursive" queries, where a SELECT statement can draw
1451         upon the set of rows that have previously been selected.
1452 
1453         CTEs can also be applied to DML constructs UPDATE, INSERT
1454         and DELETE on some databases, both as a source of CTE rows
1455         when combined with RETURNING, as well as a consumer of
1456         CTE rows.
1457 
1458         SQLAlchemy detects :class:`.CTE` objects, which are treated
1459         similarly to :class:`.Alias` objects, as special elements
1460         to be delivered to the FROM clause of the statement as well
1461         as to a WITH clause at the top of the statement.
1462 
1463         .. versionchanged:: 1.1 Added support for UPDATE/INSERT/DELETE as
1464            CTE, CTEs added to UPDATE/INSERT/DELETE.
1465 
1466         :param name: name given to the common table expression.  Like
1467          :meth:`._FromClause.alias`, the name can be left as ``None``
1468          in which case an anonymous symbol will be used at query
1469          compile time.
1470         :param recursive: if ``True``, will render ``WITH RECURSIVE``.
1471          A recursive common table expression is intended to be used in
1472          conjunction with UNION ALL in order to derive rows
1473          from those already selected.
1474 
1475         The following examples include two from PostgreSQL's documentation at
1476         http://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/static/queries-with.html,
1477         as well as additional examples.
1478 
1479         Example 1, non recursive::
1480 
1481             from sqlalchemy import (Table, Column, String, Integer,
1482                                     MetaData, select, func)
1483 
1484             metadata = MetaData()
1485 
1486             orders = Table('orders', metadata,
1487                 Column('region', String),
1488                 Column('amount', Integer),
1489                 Column('product', String),
1490                 Column('quantity', Integer)
1491             )
1492 
1493             regional_sales = select([
1494                                 orders.c.region,
1495                                 func.sum(orders.c.amount).label('total_sales')
1496                             ]).group_by(orders.c.region).cte("regional_sales")
1497 
1498 
1499             top_regions = select([regional_sales.c.region]).\
1500                     where(
1501                         regional_sales.c.total_sales >
1502                         select([
1503                             func.sum(regional_sales.c.total_sales)/10
1504                         ])
1505                     ).cte("top_regions")
1506 
1507             statement = select([
1508                         orders.c.region,
1509                         orders.c.product,
1510                         func.sum(orders.c.quantity).label("product_units"),
1511                         func.sum(orders.c.amount).label("product_sales")
1512                 ]).where(orders.c.region.in_(
1513                     select([top_regions.c.region])
1514                 )).group_by(orders.c.region, orders.c.product)
1515 
1516             result = conn.execute(statement).fetchall()
1517 
1518         Example 2, WITH RECURSIVE::
1519 
1520             from sqlalchemy import (Table, Column, String, Integer,
1521                                     MetaData, select, func)
1522 
1523             metadata = MetaData()
1524 
1525             parts = Table('parts', metadata,
1526                 Column('part', String),
1527                 Column('sub_part', String),
1528                 Column('quantity', Integer),
1529             )
1530 
1531             included_parts = select([
1532                                 parts.c.sub_part,
1533                                 parts.c.part,
1534                                 parts.c.quantity]).\
1535                                 where(parts.c.part=='our part').\
1536                                 cte(recursive=True)
1537 
1538 
1539             incl_alias = included_parts.alias()
1540             parts_alias = parts.alias()
1541             included_parts = included_parts.union_all(
1542                 select([
1543                     parts_alias.c.sub_part,
1544                     parts_alias.c.part,
1545                     parts_alias.c.quantity
1546                 ]).
1547                     where(parts_alias.c.part==incl_alias.c.sub_part)
1548             )
1549 
1550             statement = select([
1551                         included_parts.c.sub_part,
1552                         func.sum(included_parts.c.quantity).
1553                           label('total_quantity')
1554                     ]).\
1555                     group_by(included_parts.c.sub_part)
1556 
1557             result = conn.execute(statement).fetchall()
1558 
1559         Example 3, an upsert using UPDATE and INSERT with CTEs::
1560 
1561             from datetime import date
1562             from sqlalchemy import (MetaData, Table, Column, Integer,
1563                                     Date, select, literal, and_, exists)
1564 
1565             metadata = MetaData()
1566 
1567             visitors = Table('visitors', metadata,
1568                 Column('product_id', Integer, primary_key=True),
1569                 Column('date', Date, primary_key=True),
1570                 Column('count', Integer),
1571             )
1572 
1573             # add 1 visitors for the product_id == 1
1574             product_id = 1
1575             day = date.today()
1576             count = 1
1577 
1578             update_cte = (
1579                 visitors.update()
1580                 .where(and_(visitors.c.product_id == product_id,
1581                             visitors.c.date == day))
1582                 .values(count=visitors.c.count + count)
1583                 .returning(literal(1))
1584                 .cte('update_cte')
1585             )
1586 
1587             upsert = visitors.insert().from_select(
1588                 [visitors.c.product_id, visitors.c.date, visitors.c.count],
1589                 select([literal(product_id), literal(day), literal(count)])
1590                     .where(~exists(update_cte.select()))
1591             )
1592 
1593             connection.execute(upsert)
1594 
1595         .. seealso::
1596 
1597             :meth:`.orm.query.Query.cte` - ORM version of
1598             :meth:`.HasCTE.cte`.
1599 
1600         """
1601         return CTE(self, name=name, recursive=recursive)

1796     @classmethod
1797     def parse_legacy_select(self, arg):
1798         """Parse the for_update argument of :func:`.select`.
1799 
1800         :param mode: Defines the lockmode to use.
1801 
1802             ``None`` - translates to no lockmode
1803 
1804             ``'update'`` - translates to ``FOR UPDATE``
1805             (standard SQL, supported by most dialects)
1806 
1807             ``'nowait'`` - translates to ``FOR UPDATE NOWAIT``
1808             (supported by Oracle, PostgreSQL 8.1 upwards)
1809 
1810             ``'read'`` - translates to ``LOCK IN SHARE MODE`` (for MySQL),
1811             and ``FOR SHARE`` (for PostgreSQL)
1812 
1813             ``'read_nowait'`` - translates to ``FOR SHARE NOWAIT``
1814             (supported by PostgreSQL). ``FOR SHARE`` and
1815             ``FOR SHARE NOWAIT`` (PostgreSQL).
1816 
1817         """
1818         if arg in (None, False):
1819             return None
1820 
1821         nowait = read = False
1822         if arg == 'nowait':
1823             nowait = True
1824         elif arg == 'read':
1825             read = True
1826         elif arg == 'read_nowait':
1827             read = nowait = True
1828         elif arg is not True:
1829             raise exc.ArgumentError("Unknown for_update argument: %r" % arg)
1830 
1831         return ForUpdateArg(read=read, nowait=nowait)
1832 
1833     @property
1834     def legacy_for_update_value(self):
1835         if self.read and not self.nowait:
1836             return "read"
1837         elif self.read and self.nowait:
1838             return "read_nowait"
1839         elif self.nowait:
1840             return "nowait"
1841         else:
1842             return True
1843 
1844     def __eq__(self, other):
1845         return (
1846             isinstance(other, ForUpdateArg) and
1847             other.nowait == self.nowait and
1848             other.read == self.read and
1849             other.skip_locked == self.skip_locked and
1850             other.key_share == self.key_share and
1851             other.of is self.of
1852         )

1854     def __hash__(self):
1855         return id(self)
1856

1858         if self.of is not None:
1859             self.of = [clone(col, **kw) for col in self.of]
1860 
1861     def __init__(
1862             self, nowait=False, read=False, of=None,

1868         """

2769         seen = set()
2770         translate = self._from_cloned
2771 
2772         for item in itertools.chain(
2773             _from_objects(*self._raw_columns),
2774             _from_objects(self._whereclause)
2775             if self._whereclause is not None else (),
2776             self._from_obj
2777         ):

2779                 raise exc.InvalidRequestError(
2780                     "select() construct refers to itself as a FROM")
2781             if translate and item in translate:
2782                 item = translate[item]

2785             seen.update(item._cloned_set)

2789     def _get_display_froms(self, explicit_correlate_froms=None,
2790                            implicit_correlate_froms=None):
2791         """Return the full list of 'from' clauses to be displayed.
2792 
2793         Takes into account a set of existing froms which may be
2794         rendered in the FROM clause of enclosing selects; this Select
2795         may want to leave those absent if it is automatically
2796         correlating.
2797 
2798         """
2799         froms = self._froms
2800 
2801         toremove = set(itertools.chain(*[
2802             _expand_cloned(f._hide_froms)
2803             for f in froms]))
2804         if toremove:
2805             # if we're maintaining clones of froms,
2806             # add the copies out to the toremove list.  only include
2807             # clones that are lexical equivalents.
2808             if self._from_cloned:
2809                 toremove.update(
2810                     self._from_cloned[f] for f in
2811                     toremove.intersection(self._from_cloned)
2812                     if self._from_cloned[f]._is_lexical_equivalent(f)
2813                 )
2814             # filter out to FROM clauses not in the list,
2815             # using a list to maintain ordering
2816             froms = [f for f in froms if f not in toremove]
2817 
2818         if self._correlate:
2819             to_correlate = self._correlate
2820             if to_correlate:
2821                 froms = [
2822                     f for f in froms if f not in
2823                     _cloned_intersection(
2824                         _cloned_intersection(
2825                             froms, explicit_correlate_froms or ()),
2826                         to_correlate
2827                     )
2828                 ]
2829 
2830         if self._correlate_except is not None:
2831 
2832             froms = [
2833                 f for f in froms if f not in
2834                 _cloned_difference(
2835                     _cloned_intersection(
2836                         froms, explicit_correlate_froms or ()),
2837                     self._correlate_except
2838                 )
2839             ]
2840 
2841         if self._auto_correlate and \
2842                 implicit_correlate_froms and \
2843                 len(froms) > 1:
2844 
2845             froms = [
2846                 f for f in froms if f not in
2847                 _cloned_intersection(froms, implicit_correlate_froms)
2848             ]
2849 
2850             if not len(froms):
2851                 raise exc.InvalidRequestError("Select statement '%s"

2982     def _copy_internals(self, clone=_clone, **kw):
2983         super(Select, self)._copy_internals(clone, **kw)
2984 
2985         # Select() object has been cloned and probably adapted by the
2986         # given clone function.  Apply the cloning function to internal
2987         # objects
2988 
2989         # 1. keep a dictionary of the froms we've cloned, and what
2990         # they've become.  This is consulted later when we derive
2991         # additional froms from "whereclause" and the columns clause,
2992         # which may still reference the uncloned parent table.
2993         # as of 0.7.4 we also put the current version of _froms, which
2994         # gets cleared on each generation.  previously we were "baking"
2995         # _froms into self._from_obj.
2996         self._from_cloned = from_cloned = dict(
2997             (f, clone(f, **kw)) for f in self._from_obj.union(self._froms))
2998 
2999         # 3. update persistent _from_obj with the cloned versions.
3000         self._from_obj = util.OrderedSet(from_cloned[f] for f in
3001                                          self._from_obj)
3002 
3003         # the _correlate collection is done separately, what can happen
3004         # here is the same item is _correlate as in _from_obj but the
3005         # _correlate version has an annotation on it - (specifically
3006         # RelationshipProperty.Comparator._criterion_exists() does
3007         # this). Also keep _correlate liberally open with its previous
3008         # contents, as this set is used for matching, not rendering.
3009         self._correlate = set(clone(f) for f in
3010                               self._correlate).union(self._correlate)
3011 
3012         # 4. clone other things.   The difficulty here is that Column
3013         # objects are not actually cloned, and refer to their original
3014         # .table, resulting in the wrong "from" parent after a clone
3015         # operation.  Hence _from_cloned and _from_obj supersede what is
3016         # present here.
3017         self._raw_columns = [clone(c, **kw) for c in self._raw_columns]
3018         for attr in '_whereclause', '_having', '_order_by_clause', \
3019                 '_group_by_clause', '_for_update_arg':
3020             if getattr(self, attr) is not None:
3021                 setattr(self, attr, clone(getattr(self, attr), **kw))
3022 
3023         # erase exported column list, _froms collection,
3024         # etc.
3025         self._reset_exported()

3085     @_generative
3086     def with_only_columns(self, columns):
3087         r"""Return a new :func:`.select` construct with its columns
3088         clause replaced with the given columns.
3089 
3090         This method is exactly equivalent to as if the original
3091         :func:`.select` had been called with the given columns
3092         clause.   I.e. a statement::
3093 
3094             s = select([table1.c.a, table1.c.b])
3095             s = s.with_only_columns([table1.c.b])
3096 
3097         should be exactly equivalent to::
3098 
3099             s = select([table1.c.b])
3100 
3101         This means that FROM clauses which are only derived
3102         from the column list will be discarded if the new column
3103         list no longer contains that FROM::
3104 
3105             >>> table1 = table('t1', column('a'), column('b'))
3106             >>> table2 = table('t2', column('a'), column('b'))
3107             >>> s1 = select([table1.c.a, table2.c.b])
3108             >>> print s1
3109             SELECT t1.a, t2.b FROM t1, t2
3110             >>> s2 = s1.with_only_columns([table2.c.b])
3111             >>> print s2
3112             SELECT t2.b FROM t1
3113 
3114         The preferred way to maintain a specific FROM clause
3115         in the construct, assuming it won't be represented anywhere
3116         else (i.e. not in the WHERE clause, etc.) is to set it using
3117         :meth:`.Select.select_from`::
3118 
3119             >>> s1 = select([table1.c.a, table2.c.b]).\
3120             ...         select_from(table1.join(table2,
3121             ...                 table1.c.a==table2.c.a))
3122             >>> s2 = s1.with_only_columns([table2.c.b])
3123             >>> print s2
3124             SELECT t2.b FROM t1 JOIN t2 ON t1.a=t2.a
3125 
3126         Care should also be taken to use the correct
3127         set of column objects passed to :meth:`.Select.with_only_columns`.
3128         Since the method is essentially equivalent to calling the
3129         :func:`.select` construct in the first place with the given
3130         columns, the columns passed to :meth:`.Select.with_only_columns`
3131         should usually be a subset of those which were passed
3132         to the :func:`.select` construct, not those which are available
3133         from the ``.c`` collection of that :func:`.select`.  That
3134         is::
3135 
3136             s = select([table1.c.a, table1.c.b]).select_from(table1)
3137             s = s.with_only_columns([table1.c.b])
3138 
3139         and **not**::
3140 
3141             # usually incorrect
3142             s = s.with_only_columns([s.c.b])
3143 
3144         The latter would produce the SQL::
3145 
3146             SELECT b
3147             FROM (SELECT t1.a AS a, t1.b AS b
3148             FROM t1), t1
3149 
3150         Since the :func:`.select` construct is essentially being
3151         asked to select both from ``table1`` as well as itself.
3152 
3153         """
3154         self._reset_exported()
3155         rc = []
3156         for c in columns:
3157             c = _interpret_as_column_or_from(c)
3158             if isinstance(c, ScalarSelect):
3159                 c = c.self_group(against=operators.comma_op)
3160             rc.append(c)
3161         self._raw_columns = rc
3162

3233     @_generative
3234     def correlate(self, *fromclauses):
3235         r"""return a new :class:`.Select` which will correlate the given FROM
3236         clauses to that of an enclosing :class:`.Select`.
3237 
3238         Calling this method turns off the :class:`.Select` object's
3239         default behavior of "auto-correlation".  Normally, FROM elements
3240         which appear in a :class:`.Select` that encloses this one via
3241         its :term:`WHERE clause`, ORDER BY, HAVING or
3242         :term:`columns clause` will be omitted from this :class:`.Select`
3243         object's :term:`FROM clause`.
3244         Setting an explicit correlation collection using the
3245         :meth:`.Select.correlate` method provides a fixed list of FROM objects
3246         that can potentially take place in this process.
3247 
3248         When :meth:`.Select.correlate` is used to apply specific FROM clauses
3249         for correlation, the FROM elements become candidates for
3250         correlation regardless of how deeply nested this :class:`.Select`
3251         object is, relative to an enclosing :class:`.Select` which refers to
3252         the same FROM object.  This is in contrast to the behavior of
3253         "auto-correlation" which only correlates to an immediate enclosing
3254         :class:`.Select`.   Multi-level correlation ensures that the link
3255         between enclosed and enclosing :class:`.Select` is always via
3256         at least one WHERE/ORDER BY/HAVING/columns clause in order for
3257         correlation to take place.

3259         If ``None`` is passed, the :class:`.Select` object will correlate
3260         none of its FROM entries, and all will render unconditionally
3261         in the local FROM clause.
3262 
3263         :param \*fromclauses: a list of one or more :class:`.FromClause`
3264          constructs, or other compatible constructs (i.e. ORM-mapped
3265          classes) to become part of the correlate collection.
3266

3268             :meth:`.Select.correlate`.
3269 
3270         .. versionchanged:: 0.8.0 The :meth:`.Select.correlate` method no
3271            longer unconditionally removes entries from the FROM clause;
3272            instead, the candidate FROM entries must also be matched by a FROM
3273            entry located in an enclosing :class:`.Select`, which ultimately
3274            encloses this one as present in the WHERE clause, ORDER BY clause,

3277         .. versionchanged:: 0.8.2 explicit correlation takes place

# Idiom 655 (use-requirement-markings-for-typed-dict)

Definition: Checks for cases where required or not required markings can be used to simplify TypedDict classes.

Rationale: Creation of multiple subclasses to accomodate optional keys in TypedDict with a base class containing required keys leads to inefficient design and duplicated code that negatively impacts maintainability.

Example:
class _MovieBase(TypedDict):  # implicitly total=True
    title: str

class Movie(_MovieBase, total=False):
    year: int

class Movie(TypedDict):
    title: str
    year: NotRequired[int]

def trace(name, info=None, hide_args=False, allow_multiple_trace=True):
    """Trace decorator for functions.

    Very useful if you would like to add trace point on existing function:

    >>  @profiler.trace("my_point")
    >>  def my_func(self, some_args):
    >>      #code

    :param name: The name of action. E.g. wsgi, rpc, db, etc..
    :param info: Dictionary with extra trace information. For example in wsgi
                 it can be url, in rpc - message or in db sql - request.
    :param hide_args: Don't push to trace info args and kwargs. Quite useful
                      if you have some info in args that you wont to share,
                      e.g. passwords.
    :param allow_multiple_trace: If the wrapped function has already been
                                 traced either allow the new trace to occur
                                 or raise a value error denoting that multiple
                                 tracing is not allowed (by default allow).
    """
    if not info:
        info = {}
    else:
        info = info.copy()
    info["function"] = {}

    def decorator(f):
        trace_times = getattr(f, "__traced__", 0)
        if not allow_multiple_trace and trace_times:
            raise ValueError("Function '%s' has already"
                             " been traced %s times" % (f, trace_times))

        try:
            f.__traced__ = trace_times + 1
        except AttributeError:
            # Tries to work around the following:
            #
            # AttributeError: 'instancemethod' object has no
            # attribute '__traced__'
            try:
                f.im_func.__traced__ = trace_times + 1
            except AttributeError:  # nosec
                pass

        @functools.wraps(f)
        def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
            if "name" not in info["function"]:
                # Get this once (as it should **not** be changing in
                # subsequent calls).
                info["function"]["name"] = reflection.get_callable_name(f)

            if not hide_args:
                info["function"]["args"] = str(args)
                info["function"]["kwargs"] = str(kwargs)

            with Trace(name, info=info):
                return f(*args, **kwargs)

        return wrapper

    return decorator


def trace_cls(name, info=None, hide_args=False,
              trace_private=False, allow_multiple_trace=True,
              trace_class_methods=False, trace_static_methods=False):
    """Trace decorator for instances of class .

    Very useful if you would like to add trace point on existing method:

    >>  @profiler.trace_cls("rpc")
    >>  RpcManagerClass(object):
    >>
    >>      def my_method(self, some_args):
    >>          pass
    >>
    >>      def my_method2(self, some_arg1, some_arg2, kw=None, kw2=None)
    >>          pass
    >>

    :param name: The name of action. E.g. wsgi, rpc, db, etc..
    :param info: Dictionary with extra trace information. For example in wsgi
                 it can be url, in rpc - message or in db sql - request.
    :param hide_args: Don't push to trace info args and kwargs. Quite useful
                      if you have some info in args that you wont to share,
                      e.g. passwords.
    :param trace_private: Trace methods that starts with "_". It wont trace
                          methods that starts "__" even if it is turned on.
    :param trace_static_methods: Trace staticmethods. This may be prone to
                                 issues so careful usage is recommended (this
                                 is also why this defaults to false).
    :param trace_class_methods: Trace classmethods. This may be prone to
                                issues so careful usage is recommended (this
                                is also why this defaults to false).
    :param allow_multiple_trace: If wrapped attributes have already been
                                 traced either allow the new trace to occur
                                 or raise a value error denoting that multiple
                                 tracing is not allowed (by default allow).
    """

    def trace_checker(attr_name, to_be_wrapped):
        if attr_name.startswith("__"):
            # Never trace really private methods.
            return (False, None)
        if not trace_private and attr_name.startswith("_"):
            return (False, None)
        if isinstance(to_be_wrapped, staticmethod):
            if not trace_static_methods:
                return (False, None)
            return (True, staticmethod)
        if isinstance(to_be_wrapped, classmethod):
            if not trace_class_methods:
                return (False, None)
            return (True, classmethod)
        return (True, None)

    def decorator(cls):
        clss = cls if inspect.isclass(cls) else cls.__class__
        mro_dicts = [c.__dict__ for c in inspect.getmro(clss)]
        traceable_attrs = []
        traceable_wrappers = []
        for attr_name, attr in inspect.getmembers(cls):
            if not (inspect.ismethod(attr) or inspect.isfunction(attr)):
                continue
            wrapped_obj = None
            for cls_dict in mro_dicts:
                if attr_name in cls_dict:
                    wrapped_obj = cls_dict[attr_name]
                    break
            should_wrap, wrapper = trace_checker(attr_name, wrapped_obj)
            if not should_wrap:
                continue
            traceable_attrs.append((attr_name, attr))
            traceable_wrappers.append(wrapper)
        if not allow_multiple_trace:
            # Check before doing any other further work (so we don't
            # halfway trace this class).
            _ensure_no_multiple_traced(traceable_attrs)
        for i, (attr_name, attr) in enumerate(traceable_attrs):
            wrapped_method = trace(name, info=info, hide_args=hide_args)(attr)
            wrapper = traceable_wrappers[i]
            if wrapper is not None:
                wrapped_method = wrapper(wrapped_method)
            setattr(cls, attr_name, wrapped_method)
        return cls

    return decorator


class TracedMeta(type):
    """Metaclass to comfortably trace all children of a specific class.

    Possible usage:

    >>>  @six.add_metaclass(profiler.TracedMeta)
    >>>  class RpcManagerClass(object):
    >>>      __trace_args__ = {'name': 'rpc',
    >>>                        'info': None,
    >>>                        'hide_args': False,
    >>>                        'trace_private': False}
    >>>
    >>>      def my_method(self, some_args):
    >>>          pass
    >>>
    >>>      def my_method2(self, some_arg1, some_arg2, kw=None, kw2=None)
    >>>          pass

    Adding of this metaclass requires to set __trace_args__ attribute to the
    class we want to modify. __trace_args__ is the dictionary with one
    mandatory key included - "name", that will define name of action to be
    traced - E.g. wsgi, rpc, db, etc...
    """
    def __init__(cls, cls_name, bases, attrs):
        super(TracedMeta, cls).__init__(cls_name, bases, attrs)

        trace_args = dict(getattr(cls, "__trace_args__", {}))
        trace_private = trace_args.pop("trace_private", False)
        allow_multiple_trace = trace_args.pop("allow_multiple_trace", True)
        if "name" not in trace_args:
            raise TypeError("Please specify __trace_args__ class level "
                            "dictionary attribute with mandatory 'name' key - "
                            "e.g. __trace_args__ = {'name': 'rpc'}")

        traceable_attrs = []
        for attr_name, attr_value in attrs.items():
            if not (inspect.ismethod(attr_value) or
                    inspect.isfunction(attr_value)):
                continue
            if attr_name.startswith("__"):
                continue
            if not trace_private and attr_name.startswith("_"):
                continue
            traceable_attrs.append((attr_name, attr_value))
        if not allow_multiple_trace:
            # Check before doing any other further work (so we don't
            # halfway trace this class).
            _ensure_no_multiple_traced(traceable_attrs)
        for attr_name, attr_value in traceable_attrs:
            setattr(cls, attr_name, trace(**trace_args)(getattr(cls,
                                                                attr_name)))


class Trace(object):

    def __init__(self, name, info=None):
        """With statement way to use profiler start()/stop().


        >> with profiler.Trace("rpc", info={"any": "values"})
        >>    some code

        instead of

        >> profiler.start()
        >> try:
        >>    your code
        >> finally:
              profiler.stop()
        """
        self._name = name
        self._info = info

    def __enter__(self):
        start(self._name, info=self._info)

    def __exit__(self, etype, value, traceback):
        if etype:
            info = {"etype": reflection.get_class_name(etype)}
            stop(info=info)
        else:
            stop()


class _Profiler(object):

    def __init__(self, hmac_key, base_id=None, parent_id=None,
                 connection_str=None, project=None, service=None):
        self.hmac_key = hmac_key
        if not base_id:
            base_id = str(uuidutils.generate_uuid())
        self._trace_stack = collections.deque([base_id, parent_id or base_id])
        self._name = collections.deque()
        self._host = socket.gethostname()
        self._connection_str = connection_str
        self._project = project
        self._service = service

    def get_base_id(self):
        """Return base id of a trace.

        Base id is the same for all elements in one trace. It's main goal is
        to be able to retrieve by one request all trace elements from storage.
        """
        return self._trace_stack[0]

    def get_parent_id(self):
        """Returns parent trace element id."""
        return self._trace_stack[-2]

    def get_id(self):
        """Returns current trace element id."""
        return self._trace_stack[-1]

    def start(self, name, info=None):
        """Start new event.

        Adds new trace_id to trace stack and sends notification
        to collector (may be ceilometer). With "info" and 3 ids:
        base_id - to be able to retrieve all trace elements by one query
        parent_id - to build tree of events (not just a list)
        trace_id - current event id.

        :param name: name of trace element (db, wsgi, rpc, etc..)
        :param info: Dictionary with any useful information related to this
                     trace element. (sql request, rpc message or url...)
        """

        info = info or {}
        info["host"] = self._host
        info["project"] = self._project
        info["service"] = self._service
        self._name.append(name)
        self._trace_stack.append(str(uuidutils.generate_uuid()))
        self._notify("%s-start" % name, info)

    def stop(self, info=None):
        """Finish latest event.

        Same as a start, but instead of pushing trace_id to stack it pops it.

        :param info: Dict with useful info. It will be send in notification.
        """
        info = info or {}
        info["host"] = self._host
        info["project"] = self._project
        info["service"] = self._service
        self._notify("%s-stop" % self._name.pop(), info)
        self._trace_stack.pop()

    def _notify(self, name, info):
        payload = {
            "name": name,
            "base_id": self.get_base_id(),
            "trace_id": self.get_id(),
            "parent_id": self.get_parent_id(),
            "timestamp": datetime.datetime.utcnow().strftime(
                "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S.%f"),
        }
        if info:
            payload["info"] = info

        notifier.notify(payload)
